title: The shadows point the wrong way
claim: The shadows aren't parallel, there were multiple studio lights.
test: Fit sun-at-infinity vs studio-lamp models to every shadow line in the two most-cited frames, then checked the fitted sun elevation against the JPL ephemeris.
headline: Every shadow line converges at one point on the horizon (chi²/dof ~1.4), and the Apollo 11 frame's fitted sun elevation of 15.7° ± 1.1° matches the JPL ephemeris value of 15.00°.
detail: Perspective makes parallel 3D shadows diverge on film, the rigorous test is where the lines converge. In both canonical frames the free-fit convergence point lands on the horizon (a lamp's would sit 4-16° below it), a lamp within ~224 m is excluded at 95% for the Apollo 11 frame, and the elevation recovered from the shadow of Armstrong's own camera matches JPL Horizons for 1969-07-21 04:43:31 UTC to 0.7° ± 1.1°.
falsification: Shadow lines sharing no single convergence point, a convergence point degrees below the horizon, or a fitted sun elevation contradicting the ephemeris would have supported studio lighting.
figureAlt: The two famous Apollo photos with digitized shadow lines extended as dashed rays converging on a single starred vanishing point at the horizon.

title: Aldrin glows in the LM's shadow
claim: Aldrin's in full shadow but clearly lit, someone aimed a fill lamp at him.
test: Computed the sunlight bounced off the regolith onto Aldrin using NASA's Hapke reflectance maps and compared the predicted suit brightness to the actual photo.
headline: Physics predicts the shadowed suit at 40% of sunlit-ground brightness [22-72%]; the photo measures 26%, if anything slightly less light than the regolith bounce alone supplies.
detail: The sunlit regolith three meters from Aldrin's boots is the fill light: Hapke parameters read from NASA's LROC maps for the actual Tranquility Base map cell predict 4.8 W/m² of bounce on his torso, 0.4% of direct sun, enough because white Beta cloth is ~7x more reflective than regolith. The measured brightness gradient down his body (boots dark, PLSS bright) and the near-black shadow floor match ground bounce and are the opposite of what a fill lamp produces.
falsification: A shadowed suit brighter than sun + regolith bounce + spacecraft interreflection can deliver, or a lit-up shadow floor, would have meant something else was lighting him.
figureAlt: AS11-40-5869, Aldrin descending the LM ladder, with red boxes marking the measured patches: sky, suit, sunlit ground, and deep-shadow ground.

title: The reused mountain backdrop
claim: Two photos from different spots show identical mountains, a reused painted backdrop.
test: Registered the two 'identical background' Apollo 15 frames with SIFT and measured how much the mountains shrink and shear between the two camera stations.
headline: The 'identical' mountains shrink 3.5-9.5% across the 1.3 km between camera stations, putting them 10-34 km away, excluding a backdrop at 30 m by at least 345x in distance.
detail: SIFT registration locks the two mountain bands together with 17 strict inliers while the foregrounds share nothing (3 of 68 candidate matches, chance level). The background also carries 1.05° of internally layered depth parallax with the correct sign ordering, real terrain at ~15/27/50+ km, where a flat painting would carry exactly zero; the same pipeline on a same-station control pair finds nothing.
falsification: Zero background parallax across the 1.3 km baseline, or a background moving as one flat sheet (an exact homography), would have supported a painted backdrop.
figureAlt: Animated blink of the two 'identical background' Apollo 15 frames aligned: the same real mountains, with the Lunar Module present in one frame and gone in the other.

title: Photos too perfect to be real
claim: Perfectly framed shots from a chest camera with no viewfinder? Impossible, a studio shot them.
test: Scored all 687 consecutive frames of five complete Hasselblad magazines for exposure, blur, framing, and horizon tilt, nothing hand-picked.
headline: 7.1% of 687 consecutive frames are outright duds and 1 in 5 detectable horizons is tilted more than 10°, even the Aldrin portrait's raw horizon leans ~15°, fixed only by cropping.
detail: Survivorship bias, quantified: five complete magazines from four missions contain black frames, sun-blasted washouts, and blurred aimless shots, a 7.1% dud rate that rises to 12.9% by Apollo 17. The nine icons the claim is built on sit at a median quality percentile of 50.5: keepers picked from a wide, human distribution, not statistical miracles, and NASA's own archive publishes the outtake reel no hoax studio would have manufactured.
falsification: A systematic sample of the archive that was uniformly excellent, no bad-frame tail for curation to hide, would have left the 'too good' claim standing.
figureAlt: Contact-sheet montage of the 48 worst NASA frames, black frames, lens-flare washouts, blurred cabin shots, each labeled with its frame ID.

title: The prop rock marked 'C'
claim: There's a letter 'C' on that rock, a props-department inventory mark.
test: Registered ten independently archived generations of AS16-107-17446, from original-film scans to the hoax sites' own crop, and measured the 'C' in each.
headline: The 'C' is absent from every scan of the original flight film; it exists in exactly one print generation, where a high-res re-scan resolves it as a ~1 mm curled fiber with a tail.
detail: Ten archive generations of the frame were registered to sub-pixel accuracy, from a 14,160-px scan of the original flight film (C contrast 2.2%, bare rock) to the hoax sites' own crop (15.5%, arc coherence 0.99). The mark exists only downstream of one print generation, is completely unmodulated by the rock surface it supposedly sits on (correlation −0.01), and at high resolution resolves into a curled fiber with a protruding tail, accompanied by a second hair in the same crop.
falsification: A 'C' present in the earliest-generation scans of the original flight film, modulated by the rock's texture and lighting, would have supported a photographed prop mark.
figureAlt: The same patch of the Apollo 16 'C rock' across ten archive generations: bare rock in every film scan, the fiber 'C' present only in one print lineage.

title: Slow-motion Earth gravity
claim: It's Earth footage slowed down 2.46x to fake lunar gravity.
test: Tracked the Apollo 15 hammer-feather drop frame by frame, then tested the 2.46x slow-down against the same clip's synced audio and the feather's drag physics.
headline: The feather falls at g = 1.22 ± 1.4 m/s², lunar; a 2.46x slow-down would need Scott speaking 9.9 syllables/s and the feather hitting ~4x faster than Earth air allows.
detail: Ballistics alone cannot separate the Moon from slowed Earth footage, that degeneracy is the claim's whole point, so the test uses the same clip's PTS-synced audio and drag physics. Scott's 144-syllable Galileo monologue matches the mission transcript in real time (4.0 syllables/s; the hoax needs 9.9 sustained), and the feather crosses its final tracked step at 2.35 ± 0.48 m/s, about 4x faster than any feather falling through Earth air could appear at 1/2.46 playback, with no terminal-velocity flattening anywhere in its fall.
falsification: A single global 2.46x factor consistently explaining the ballistics, the synced speech tempo, and the feather's drag signature would have supported slowed Earth footage.
figureAlt: Frame from the Apollo 15 TV clip of the hammer-feather drop with the tracked hammer and feather positions marked and Scott's height as the scale bar.

title: Astronauts on hidden wires
claim: Those floaty jumps are stage flying, the astronauts hung from wires.
test: Fit free-fall physics to John Young's jump salute at sub-pixel precision and searched above his helmet for any wire in a 73-frame median stack.
headline: Both jumps fit free fall at 1.69 and 1.68 ± 0.11 m/s² (lunar g = 1.62) with ~2 mm residuals, and nothing wire-like appears above the helmet down to a 0.16 mm sunlit-wire bound.
detail: Sub-pixel tracking of helmet and backpack gives constant-acceleration free fall with ~2 mm residuals, rise/fall symmetric to a few percent, and no coherent tension event above a 6 cm/s detection floor, the tiny residual structure moves helmet and backpack in opposite directions (the arm salute, not a cable). The pipeline was sensitive enough to blindly recover the clip's 2:3 telecine pulldown cadence to ~1 ms, and still found no trace of a rig.
falsification: Any rigid-body tension transient, rise/fall asymmetry, wandering g between jumps, cable-pendulum dynamics, or a visible line above the helmet would have supported a wire rig.
figureAlt: Four frames of John Young's Apollo 16 jump salute with the tracked helmet path, above the whole-clip torso-height track marking both ballistic flights.

title: The deadly Van Allen belts
claim: Nobody can cross the Van Allen belts, the radiation would've killed them.
test: Ran radiation transport along the AS-506 trajectory through NASA's AP-8/AE-8 belt models with NIST stopping-power data and compared to the flown film badges.
headline: Computed mission dose: 2.4 mGy. Measured on the crew's film badges: 1.8 mGy. A 50% lethal dose: ~4,500 mGy, the claim is off by three orders of magnitude.
detail: The real trajectory crosses the inner proton belt in ~15 minutes at 25-40° magnetic latitude, missing the core; behind the CM's 7.5 g/cm² of shielding the belt transits contribute just 0.47 mGy of the 2.4 mGy mission total. Even parked dead-center in the inner-belt core, the crew would have needed ~52 hours to reach LD50, and eleven missions of flown dosimetry (1.6-11.4 mGy) agree with the physics.
falsification: An unavoidable dose in the thousands of mGy for any feasible translunar trajectory and realistic spacecraft shielding would have supported the lethal-belts claim.
figureAlt: The Apollo 11 outbound and return trajectories drawn over the AP-8 proton and AE-8 electron belt flux maps, threading past the belt cores.

title: The computer was too weak
claim: A 1960s computer couldn't possibly navigate a spacecraft to the Moon.
test: Reassembled the actual Apollo 11 LM flight code from its 1969 listing and ran it in real time on a cycle-accurate AGC emulator.
headline: The 1969 source assembles to a bit-identical binary (SHA-256 match, 36/36 bank checksums) and runs at 99% of the authentic 85,333 cycles/sec using 3-5% of one laptop core.
detail: Luminary 099, the program that landed Eagle, assembles from its 1969 listing to a binary byte-identical to an independent transcription of the flown rope memory, then boots on a cycle-accurate emulator: 8,289 live i/o-channel writes in 60 seconds, the correct 2-second telemetry downlist, ~1 MB of RAM. The famous 1201/1202 alarms are right there in the source, a priority-scheduled OS shedding low-priority jobs under overload: sophistication, not weakness.
falsification: Source that failed to assemble to the historical bank checksums, or software whose demands exceeded what 1969-class hardware provides in real time, would have supported the claim.
figureAlt: Infographic comparing the Apollo Guidance Computer to a modern laptop: the entire flight program is 67.5 KB and costs 3-5% of one core to emulate.

title: 400,000 people kept the secret?
claim: Fine, thousands were in on it, big organizations keep big secrets all the time.
test: Reproduced the Grimes conspiracy-leak model number-for-number, then stress-tested it with mortality, deathbed confessions, and Soviet incentives.
headline: A 411,000-person hoax has an expected time-to-exposure of ~1.2 years and P(silence to 2026) ~ 7×10⁻²¹; the biggest core that keeps a 57-year secret is ~49 people.
detail: Reproducing Grimes (2016) to within 1% on 21 of 24 published checks, with 2 more matching the paper's printed rounding and 1 documented deviation: at leak rates calibrated from real exposed conspiracies, the hoax is pincered, faking the evidence needs at least ~874 witting participants under heroic assumptions, while the largest 57-year-silent core is ~49 (FBI-calibrated) to ~2,991 (ultra-conservative). In 10,000 agent-based runs, no core of 1,000+ ever stayed silent to 2026; 'they'd all be dead by now' backfires, because each death is a deathbed-confession opportunity.
falsification: A plausible leak-rate regime in which a core large enough to fabricate the evidence stays silent for 57 years would have kept the hoax arithmetically alive.
figureAlt: Heatmap of secret-survival probability versus conspiracy size and leak rate, with the Apollo program's 411,000 people far outside the survivable region.

title: Terrain verified by Japan's orbiter
claim: The mountains in the photos are set decoration, nobody could ever check the terrain.
test: Rendered the horizon a camera at the Apollo 15 site should see per JAXA's 2008 Kaguya elevation model and compared it with the skylines photographed in 1971.
headline: Japan's 2008 Kaguya elevation model reproduces the 1971 flag-salute skyline to 0.017° RMS (r = 0.99998), about 1.3 pixels on the film scan, at exactly the documented camera azimuth.
detail: Each photo's skyline was traced, converted to rays via the film's own reseau-grid calibration, and fit against the horizon rendered from JAXA's Kaguya Terrain Camera DEM with only camera pointing free. AS15-88-11866 lands at 0.017° RMS across 46° of panorama, 45.6x better than the best rival azimuth anywhere on the 360° circle; AS15-86-11603 corroborates at 0.208° but its minimum is shallow (1.28x over its best rival), so it supports rather than proves. Both sit on mountains the DEM shows are 17-20 km away and 3.5-4.1 km high, measured by a Japanese spacecraft 36+ years after the photographs.
falsification: Wrong ridge shapes, wrong angular heights, or a best skyline match away from the documented viewing azimuth would have supported fabricated terrain.
figureAlt: The 1971 Apollo 15 flag-salute photograph with the horizon predicted from Japan's 2008 Kaguya elevation model drawn as a dashed line riding the photographed ridge.

title: The 2.6-second echo from the Moon
claim: The 'live from the Moon' audio was actors on a sound stage in Houston.
test: Searched NASA's Houston mission tapes for CapCom's own voice returning from the Moon and measured the delay against the JPL ephemeris light time.
headline: CapCom's voice returns 2.64 ± 0.03 s after he speaks (5.0 sigma, 43 EVA transmissions); JPL Horizons predicts 2.59 s of light time for that hour. A sound stage predicts zero.
detail: CapCom's uplink played in the crew's helmets, leaked from their earphones into their live mics, and returned to Houston one full round trip later; cross-correlating 43 EVA-tape transmissions finds that faint echo at 2.64 s while ~1,500 control segments show nothing. An independent turn-taking check agrees, crews answer CapCom ~2.65 s slower than he answers them, and the echo appears only in the EVA comm configuration that physically allows it, which is itself hard to fake.
falsification: A voice-return delay at zero, a delay constant when the ephemeris says it should drift, or one inconsistent with the computed light time would have supported a sound stage.
figureAlt: Measured echo delays of CapCom's returning voice plotted over the JPL Horizons round-trip light-time curve near 2.6 seconds, far from the zero a sound stage would produce.
